entry.evidence: Therefore, it remains unknown whether a return to the climate that prevailed in the pre-industrial period will permit ice sheets and glaciers to recover

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML text (jats_text) of the published paper, with the PDF for figures

steps.action: The authors pose the question of whether glaciers can re-advance and ice shelves regrow if the climate cools after the Paris Agreement, noting that observational analogues are lacking.
steps.quote: it is unclear if a climatic reversal in a post-Paris world allows glaciers to re-advance, ice shelves to regrow

steps.action: They design the study as numerical experiments with ISSM on Petermann Glacier, a confined ice shelf, to find the climate conditions required for recovery to the 2008 state.
steps.quote: We examine the climate conditions required for Petermann to recover to its present-day (2008) state after an ice-shelf breakup and grounding-line retreat

steps.action: All recovery runs start from a retreated 2300 AD state produced in the authors' earlier projection (ref. 19) under a 2 °C ocean-only warming; atmospheric warming is ignored for simplicity.
steps.quote: which is attained as a response to a 2 °C ocean-only warming relative to present-day

steps.action: Model initialisation (Methods): basal friction and ice-shelf viscosity are inverted with an adjoint method against observed velocities, and the floating-ice calving threshold σmax is calibrated to 300 kPa by reproducing the present-day margin, following ref. 19.
steps.quote: calibrate σmax to 300 kPa for floating ice by reproducing the present-day ice-shelf margin after a 50-year transient relaxation

steps.action: Ocean forcing (Methods) is set as depth-dependent basal melt profiles taken from observations and from other groups' MITgcm modelling (Cai et al. 2017).
steps.quote: Ocean forcing is parameterised based on observations of Petermann’s ice shelf and modelling using the ocean model MITgcm

steps.action: In the first recovery suite they reverse the 2 °C ocean warming, returning basal melt rates to present-day values, and simulate the glacier's evolution.
steps.quote: thus lowering ice-shelf basal melt rates back to those associated with present-day ocean conditions

steps.action: They compare the simulated grounding line, calving front and discharge with the present-day state and the observed flux: the advance is small and discharge stays about 40% above present.
steps.quote: Despite the ocean temperature being returned to its present-day value, the grounding line and ice-shelf front of Petermann advance only ~3 and ~15 km

steps.action: They reject ocean cooling alone as a sufficient route to recovery.
steps.quote: this substantial ocean cooling alone would not cause Petermann’s ice shelf to recover

steps.action: They vary the time scale of ocean cooling from one year to centuries, and turn ocean melt off entirely (Table S1); recovery still fails.
steps.quote: recovery fails regardless of whether the ocean cools from one year to the next, or over several centuries

steps.action: They interpret the persistence of the retreated state under present-day ocean temperature as evidence of multiple equilibrium states, citing tipping-point work (ref. 32).
steps.quote: which suggests that the glacier has multiple equilibrium states

steps.action: Because ocean cooling alone failed, they pose a second rival route: ocean cooling combined with an increased surface mass balance.
steps.quote: We therefore examine whether reversed ocean temperature in combination with increased net surface mass balance can allow regrowth

steps.action: They impose an elevation-dependent positive SMB anomaly (+1 to +0.2 m w.e.) on the MAR present-day field, which resembles the pre-industrial SMB, together with ocean cooling (Methods §5.3.1).
steps.quote: we impose a positive perturbation to the model’s contemporary surface mass balance

steps.action: They reject ocean cooling plus increased SMB as a route: upstream thickening speeds up flow and raises discharge without advancing the front.
steps.quote: Petermann Glacier Ice Shelf does not regrow to its original extent

steps.action: Sensitivity tests with stronger positive SMB shifts (Methods; Table S1) also fail to produce recovery.
steps.quote: We also did sensitivity tests with even stronger shifts of the surface mass balance

steps.action: After the two failed routes, they pose reduced calving as a third route and hypothesise that it is linked to sea-ice growth and ice mélange in the fjord.
steps.quote: we consider whether reduced calving rates can aid the recovery of Petermann Glacier Ice Shelf

steps.action: They raise the von Mises calving stress threshold σmax, both alone and combined with ocean cooling, and simulate.
steps.quote: we impose changes to the calving regime by increasing the stress threshold in the calving law

steps.action: They reject reduced calving alone as a sufficient route.
steps.quote: reduced calving rates alone do not yield ice-shelf recovery

steps.action: Under combined ocean cooling and reduced calving, the shelf re-forms and the grounding line re-advances; they compare the grounding-line flux with the observed present-day flux (~9.8 Gt/a).
steps.quote: the grounding-line flux declines to its contemporary values

steps.action: They vary the speed of ocean cooling and of the calving change, and add calving seasonality (Supplement S1.1); the joint requirement holds.
steps.quote: Additional experiments confirm that this holds regardless of whether ocean cooling is rapid or sluggish

steps.action: They retain the reading that, under present-day climate, the shelf has two equilibrium configurations: long with moderate discharge, short with high discharge.
steps.quote: its ice shelf has two different equilibrium configurations

steps.action: They refine the claim to a step-like threshold: with sufficient ocean cooling, σmax above about 440 kPa triggers full advance; without ocean cooling, no σmax value works.
steps.quote: This transition has a non-linear and step-like dependence on the calving stress threshold σmax

steps.action: They set the result against earlier model studies that called the outer Petermann and 79N shelves dynamically passive, noting those studies lacked transient calving and melt.
steps.quote: recovery is unlikely unless calving rates are reduced

steps.action: They take the Holocene history of Petermann's grounding-line retreat, shelf breakup c. 6900 yr BP and regrowth from c. 2100 yr BP from sediment-core reconstructions (Reilly et al. 2019; Jakobsson et al. 2018).
steps.quote: started to grow again c. 2100 yrs BP, to reach its contemporary configuration ~600 years ago

steps.action: They compare the model framework with the reconstructed history and propose a staged Holocene scenario of ocean cooling followed by sea-ice-driven calving reduction.
steps.quote: a plausible explanation for the historic re-establishment of Petermann Glacier Ice Shelf was an ocean cooling combined with reduced calving

steps.action: They postulate a physical mechanism: sea-ice growth and a stronger ice mélange suppress calving, with σmax read as a proxy for mélange strength.
steps.quote: can be induced by sea-ice growth and changes to the ice mélange strength in Petermann Fjord

steps.action: They compare the mechanism with published Holocene sea-ice proxy records from Nares Strait (Detlef et al. 2021) and with modern sea-ice and ocean observations.
steps.quote: This hypothesis is supported by reconstructions of sea-ice and ocean conditions over the Holocene.

steps.action: They replace the Budd friction law with a Schoof law (Supplement S1.2) and find recovery similarly difficult.
steps.quote: post-breakup recovery of Petermann is similarly difficult using a Schoof friction law

steps.action: They keep the headline claim: post-breakup recovery requires major cooling plus calving suppression, and a mere reversal of ocean warming leaves discharge 40% above present.
steps.quote: post-breakup recovery of the ice shelf is difficult and requires major climatic cooling to occur

No; few observations of ice-shelf regrowth, and paleo traces of advance are sparse

Yes: ocean cooling alone; ocean cooling plus SMB; reduced calving alone; ocean cooling plus reduced calving
Yes; model runs give different recovery outcomes for each forcing pathway

Yes: cooling and calving time scales, calving seasonality, stronger SMB, melt off, Schoof friction law
Kept: only ocean cooling plus reduced calving recovers the shelf
Not assessable; review file not supplied

end.claim: In the model, Petermann's ice shelf does not recover after a future breakup under ocean cooling, increased SMB or reduced calving alone; only ocean cooling combined with reduced calving (σmax above ~440 kPa) restores it, and otherwise discharge stays ~40% above present.

decisive_move.sentence: The suite of recovery simulations under alternative forcing pathways, culminating in the combined ocean-cooling and raised-calving-threshold runs, produced the only recovering case and so the claim.

gates.evidence: Action: each simulation suite was directed by a stated candidate route to recovery (ocean cooling, plus SMB, plus reduced calving; §2.2 ¶1, §2.3 ¶1), but no field data were acquired. Claim: each route could have produced recovery in the model and the first three did not (§2.1 ¶3, §2.2 ¶2, §2.3 ¶3). The test is in silico only; the paleo comparison is a consistency check, not a test that could fail (§3.2 ¶3). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the runs.

von Mises tensile stress criterion used in the calving law

novelty_claims.quote: Therefore, it remains unknown whether a return to the climate that prevailed in the pre-industrial period will permit ice sheets and glaciers to recover

limits: Only the published paper (PDF and XML) was supplied. The peer-review reports exist (p. 9) but were not provided, so no review sequence is coded. The Supplementary Information was not supplied: checks reported in Figs. S5–S11, Table S1 and Sections S1.1–S1.2 are coded from their main-text descriptions. Inference: model initialisation and calving calibration are coded as inherited from ref. 19 because the text points there for details; whether the inversions were rerun here is not stated. 'Confirmed' holds only within a single ice-flow model (ISSM, SSA, 2D); there is no test against nature and no uncertainty quantification. Sub-claims: the σmax ~440 kPa threshold is regularity_in_range within the model for Petermann only. The sea-ice and mélange mechanism is postulated and only weakly best_explanation: it is not explicitly modelled and the authors say it is 'yet to be tested' (§3.4 ¶4). The Holocene scenario is best_explanation, supported by cited reconstructions. Transfer to Antarctic unconfined shelves is speculation. The order of experiments as written may not match the order in which they were run (inference). Composition strong_inference is applied to in-model rivals (forcing pathways), not to rival hypotheses about nature.

disagreements.target: Hill et al. 2018 (Petermann) and Rathmann et al. 2017 (79N): outer ice shelf interpreted as dynamically passive
disagreements.support: Transient simulations with explicit calving and sub-shelf melt show that loss beyond the passive ice limit makes recovery unlikely unless calving is reduced.
disagreements.quote: These model studies did, however, not include transient effects and involved feedbacks, and thus excluded explicit treatment of calving or sub-shelf melt.

disagreements.target: General notion that unconfined Antarctic ice shelves provide little buttressing (refs. 64, 66)
disagreements.support: Cited work showing sea ice can raise effective shelf viscosity and buttressing, and that sea-ice loss coincides with shelf disintegration; no new evidence is offered here.
disagreements.quote: The general notion is that the laterally extensive, unconfined ice shelves typical for present-day Antarctica provide little buttressing to upstream ice

alternatives_considered.reason: Budd's effective-pressure form allows a smooth basal-stress transition in the grounding zone, shown to improve the fit with remote sensing data

alternatives_considered.alternatives: other calving laws compared for Greenland glaciers (ref. 52)
alternatives_considered.reason: found by Choi et al. 2018 to give the most realistic behaviour

alternatives_considered.chosen: Present-day MAR SMB shifted by elevation-dependent positive anomalies
alternatives_considered.alternatives: SMB products from model intercomparisons such as ISMIP6, combined with a regional SMB model
alternatives_considered.reason: none given (described as relatively simple); stronger shifts also fail

alternatives_considered.chosen: Linear depth-dependent basal melt parameterisation from MITgcm results
alternatives_considered.alternatives: more elaborate ocean parameterisations (e.g. PICO, PICOP; refs. 59, 60)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Ocean-only warming to reach the retreated state
alternatives_considered.reason: ignored for simplicity; ocean melt causes ~80% of current mass loss

alternatives_considered.chosen: Instantaneous (flip-switch) changes in ocean temperature and calving
